The schooner Sea Gull rolled heavily in the gray troughs fifty miles south-southeast of Cape Race. Captain MacIntyre stood wedged between the binnacle and the starboard rail, clutching his brass sextant in frostbitten fingers as foaming crests broke over the bulwarks, washing six barrels of whale oil loose across the slippery deck. The second mate and three green hands scrambled through freezing seawater to secure the thrashing hogsheads before they stove in the companionway hatch.

By the final week of August, the heat in the river bottoms becomes a physical weight, thick as warm syrup and buzzing with the electric crescendo of periodical cicadas. From high in the canopy of the shagbark hickories, their collective chorus rises and crests like ocean surf breaking against invisible shoals, filling the humid twilight with an urgent, droning hymn that marks the inevitable dying down of another Midwestern summer.
